text:
Although much of the Southeast experienced very cold weather (temperatures averaged more than 8F below normal) and little or no precipitation (except for light snow in the southern Appalachians and eastern North Carolina), Florida was an exception as light showers dropped 0.1 to 0.7 inches of rain on south-central and eastern coastal sections. The rain limited any drought expansion, but it fell just north and west of last weeks abnormal dryness, maintaining southern Floridas D0 as the KBDI index (fire potential indicator) remained above 500 (max=800).

text:
Last weeks stormy and wet weather in the Northwest was replaced with tranquil conditions (dry and mild), courtesy of high pressure that enveloped much of the West. Most of the Far West and Southwest maintained status-quo, with the latter region experiencing short-term wetness from record high precipitation during mid-October to mid-November (water year-to-date NRCS average basin precipitation between 125 to 250% of normal). In the Cascades, however, even after last weeks heavy precipitation, many NRCS SNOTEL sites are still in the lower 10 th percentile since October 1. As of Dec. 21, even more locations are in the lower 5 th percentile (record or near-record low) for snow water content. Combined with subnormal precipitation, mild weather has further eroded the snow pack by melting, or by causing the precipitation to fall as rain instead of snow. Accordingly, D0 was added to the southern Washington and northern Oregon Cascades, reflecting a very slow start to 2004-05 water year and low snow pack.

In contrast, another week with subnormal precipitation (generally less than 0.3 inches) and above-normal temperatures (departures +10 to +15F) further decreased the average basin water year-to-date precipitation and snow water content in the northern Rockies, especially across eastern Idaho and western Montana. With much of this region in a 5-year drought, a slow start to the 2004-05 water year is focusing attention on the January 1, 2005 water supply forecast. Since October 1, less than 70% of normal precipitation has fallen on the following drainage basins in southwestern and central Montana: Headwaters Missouri mainstem (49%); Upper Clark Fork (64%); Bitterroot (66%); Jefferson (67%); and Missouri mainstem (69%). And just like the Cascades, the 2004-05 water year precipitation and Dec. 21 snow water content were in the lower 5 th percentile (near-record or record lows) in southwestern Montana. As a result, drought was expanded by 1-category in southwestern and central Montana.

text:
A major winter storm brought blizzard conditions to the Northeast on January 22-23, but produced only light rain showers in the southern Atlantic States. As a result, abnormal dryness (D0) continued in parts of southern Florida. Fort Lauderdale, FL, coming off its driest year since 1989 and ninth-driest year in more than 90 years of records, received 1.92 inches (82 percent of normal) of rain during the first 25 days of January. The fire danger, represented by the Keetch-Byram Drought Index (KBDI), remained high in southern Florida, averaging 529 (on a scale of 0 to 800) in Broward County and 502 in Martin County. KBDI values locally higher than 650 were reported in Broward and Palm Beach Counties, according to the Florida Division of Forestry. High values of the KBDI are an indication that conditions are favorable for the occurrence and spread of wildfires.

Meanwhile, rainfall deficits existed at several time scales along and near the Atlantic Coast as far north as the Carolinas. During 2004, rainfall was more than one foot below normal and less than 80 percent of normal in locations such as Savannah, GA, and Charleston, SC. This year is off to a dry start in the southern Atlantic region, with January 1-25 totals of 0.69 inch (22 percent of normal) in Savannah and 1.16 inches (36 percent) in Charleston. This section of the Atlantic Coast will need to be monitored for possible introduction of abnormal dryness.
